_comment: The Phase 4 cross-provider conformance declaration (issue #86 / WP4.5,
docs/EPIC-B-multi-nas.md section 63A and the section 72 Phase 4 TDD Gate).
Section 63A is explicit that a conformance suite must distinguish SUPPORTED,
UNSUPPORTED and NOT_APPLICABLE 'rather than silently skipping missing provider
features'. A capability that is merely absent from a result set is the failure
mode this file exists to prevent: absence reads as passing.
So every provider declares an outcome for EVERY capability. matrix_test.go
fails if a provider omits one, if a declaration names a capability that does
not exist, if a non-supported declaration carries no reason, if a blocked one
carries no tracked blocker, if a verifiedBy points at a path that is not there,
or if the repository has quietly started satisfying something declared
unsupported. The last of those is what stops this file rotting into fiction.
Every provider also declares the EPIC whose gate consumes its column. Six of
them are EPIC B's, which is what the section 72 Phase 4 Exit Gate is computed
over. UGOS is EPIC D's: its packaging is #83 (D1.2) since the UGOS split, so a
UGOS cell cannot hold Phase 4 open. It is still declared, still checked and
still reported here, on exactly the same terms as every other column, because
the check that caught UGOS claiming app-store packaging with no UPK behind it
only works while the column exists.
This file holds DECLARATIONS only. The checks that decide each cell live in
matrix_test.go, keyed by capability id, and the two lists have to agree
exactly.

capabilities.title: Core binary hash parity (this provider's own shipped bytes)
This provider's own architecture claim matches the build
State path persists outside the container
API reachable only through the intended path
Provider removal does not alter core
Removal does not delete retained backups

canonical-image-parity.reason: container/compose.yaml BUILDS the canonical image from container/Dockerfile rather than pulling a published reference. It is the source of the image the other six profiles consume, so pinning it to its own output would be circular.

core-binary-hash-parity.reason: container/ BUILDS the canonical image from container/Dockerfile rather than consuming a published one, so its binaries are compiled during the build and nothing here is a checked-in artifact to hash. The bytes are decided by the build itself, and apps/generic/tests/dockercli drives the real image the build produces.

architecture-parity.reason: This provider makes no architecture claim of its own: it names one multi-arch canonical image and lets the runtime pick. The claim that the built architecture set matches canonical.json is repository-wide and is release-manifest-integrity's row, not seven copies of itself.

no-provider-lifecycle.reason: Two reasons, both structural. apps/generic IS the canonical web host (section 37), not a wrapper around it, so there is no wrapper for a second implementation to hide in. And container/compose.yaml carries a build: key, which the scanner treats as a violation everywhere else precisely because a Tier B/C package must reuse the canonical image rather than build one; here it is the file the canonical image is built FROM.

provider-removal-preserves-core.reason: scripts/architecture/verify-ui-shared-without-provider-sdks.sh says it directly: apps/generic is the vendor-neutral baseline the default Vite build targets, so it is not a provider SDK directory and ui/shared's own tests import its bridge on purpose. The rule applies to the six vendor providers.

host-management-plane-untouched.reason: A plain Docker host has no vendor management plane, but the rule that a package installs no host unit, cron entry or config-database write still applies, and container/ is held to it like every other profile.

install-update-remove.reason: Automated rather than operator-verified: apps/generic/tests/dockercli drives the real docker CLI against the real image (section 67), so there is no hardware step to write a procedure for.

ui-launch.reason: Same as install-update-remove: covered by the Docker CLI suite and ui/shared's own tests, not by a hardware procedure.

upgrade-preserves-state.reason: No vendor updater to exercise; container replacement is what the Docker CLI suite already does.

remove-preserves-backups.reason: No vendor uninstaller to exercise. The compose profile declares no named volume, so there is nothing for `down -v` to reach.

native-auth.reason: Tier C. No identity provider on a plain Docker host; section 13A local auth is the whole story.

embedded-window.reason: Tier C. Opens in a standalone browser.

app-store-packaging.reason: Tier C. There is no store; this is the raw compose deployment.

storage-picker.reason: Tier C. Manual path entry, because no host volume API exists to browse.

package-metadata.reason: Work package 4.2's UPK was moved out of this EPIC into EPIC D and is still open as #83. apps/ugos/ contains the frontend bridge and nothing else: no project.yaml, no compose, no icon, no image tar. Until #83 lands, UGOS is the one Phase 4 Exit Gate provider with no package in this repository.

canonical-image-parity.reason: Nothing in apps/ugos/ references an image yet, so there is no reference to compare.

core-binary-hash-parity.reason: The UPK is what would carry the architecture image tars (section 41), and there is no UPK, so there is no shipped byte to hash. Unlike the six providers that consume the OCI image by reference, this one is not not-applicable: UGOS is meant to ship its own artifact, so the cell stays blocked until #83 produces one.

architecture-parity.expectedDetail: makes no architecture claim of its own
architecture-parity.reason: The UPK declares the architecture image tars (section 41); no UPK, no claim of its own to check.

state-persistence.reason: The UPK's compose declares the storage mapping (section 22); it does not exist yet.

backup-root-containment.reason: BACKUP_ROOT comes from the UPK's install parameters (section 20); they do not exist yet.

no-provider-lifecycle.reason: True but thin: apps/ugos/ is four bridge files today. It will need re-reading when #83 adds the UPK.

api-path-isolation.reason: The UPK's compose decides which container publishes a port; it does not exist yet.

install-update-remove.reason: docs/acceptance/ugos-local-notification.md covers notifications only. The install/update/disable/uninstall/reinstall procedure is work package 4.2's, and belongs with #83.

ui-launch.reason: The UI an operator would launch is the UPK's, and docs/acceptance/ugos-local-notification.md covers notifications only. Section 12's embedded provider window is delivered by the UPK too, which is why embedded-window below is blocked on the same issue rather than declared supported: both cannot be true at once.

upgrade-preserves-state.reason: Section 46's upgrade behaviour needs the package that gets upgraded.

remove-preserves-backups.reason: Section 48's uninstall behaviour needs the package that gets uninstalled.

native-auth.reason: The bridge opts in, but nothing this repository produces loads the UGOS bridge: there is no UPK (#83), and even once there is one, serve-ui embeds a single bundle chosen at build time (#180). A capability flag is a statement of intent until an installed artifact runs it.

native-notifications.reason: Same as native-auth: the flag is set in apps/ugos/frontend/platform.ts and no artifact loads that file.

embedded-window.reason: Section 12's embedded provider window is delivered by the UPK, which is exactly what ui-launch above says. Declaring this supported while blocking ui-launch on the same sentence was a contradiction: both rows are the same missing package.

app-store-packaging.expectedDetail: declares no store or catalog artifact
app-store-packaging.reason: The bridge claims it, and section 4A promises it, but no UPK exists in this repository yet. Passing on the bridge flag alone would be exactly the kind of claim the store-artifact half of this check exists to refuse.

storage-picker.reason: Same as native-auth: declared in a bridge no shipped artifact loads.

canonical-image-parity.reason: Synology is the one Phase 4 provider that cannot consume the OCI image: DSM's Package Center installs a native .spk. Section 3.7 makes the SPK a sibling of the image carrying the same core binary digest, so parity here is binary parity, not image parity.

core-binary-hash-parity.reason: The .spk is not in this repository; cmd/spkctl builds it. The byte comparison this row demands is real and it does run: spkctl verify re-derives each binary's SHA-256 out of a finished package and compares it against container/release-manifest.json, and TestVerify_BinaryHashParity is the test that proves it, including the negative case. apps/common/packaging cannot execute it without importing across the apps/synology module boundary that scripts/architecture/*.sh enforces, so this cell records where the comparison happens instead of pretending to do it here.

architecture-parity.reason: The one provider that makes an architecture claim of its own: apps/synology/spk/arch.go maps each DSM arch family to the GOARCH the release builds for it, and this row holds that list against what container/release-manifest.json actually built.

state-persistence.reason: DSM fixes the persistent location: /var/packages/<pkg>/var under the package FHS, not a bind mount this repository declares.

backup-root-containment.reason: The backup root is a DSM shared folder the operator picks at install time: conf/resource's data-share worker declares the share by name and carries no path, so there is no checked-in host path pair for this check to compare. What IS decided in this repository is the other side of the same rule, that the package places no key material or auth state anywhere (no-bundled-secrets) and that its lifecycle scripts delete nothing outside the package footprint. The containment itself is step 5 of the procedure, which puts a canary in the share and diffs a listing across the uninstall.

no-provider-lifecycle.reason: DSM's package format MANDATES preinst/postinst/preuninst/postuninst/preupgrade/postupgrade and start-stop-status. Those scripts are the platform's contract, not a lifecycle engine of our own, and apps/synology holds them to wrapper-only behaviour.

api-path-isolation.reason: Checked for real rather than excused. The previous declaration said the SPK runs one process behind DSM's own reverse proxy with the port coming from conf/resource, and both halves were false: start-stop-status starts two processes, common.sh sets UI_PORT=8477 and ENGINE_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8478, and conf/resource holds a data-share worker with no port in it at all. Synology is the one provider whose engine isolation is enforced by a shell script instead of a Docker network, so it is the weakest of the seven and the last one that should have been exempt.

native-auth.reason: Tier B. Section 4A makes DSM SSO a follow-on capability; the initial package uses section 13A local auth.

native-notifications.reason: Tier B. No DSM notification adapter in v1; webhooks instead.

embedded-window.reason: apps/synology/frontend/platform.ts opts in, but the .spk serves the same go:embed'ed bundle the canonical image does, and ui/shared/vite.config.ts defaults that bundle to the generic shell. apps/synology/README.md's first known gap says it outright and step 3.6 of the acceptance procedure tells the operator to expect the generic bridge, so recording PASS here contradicted two documents in the same tree. #180 tracks the missing serve-side selection.

app-store-packaging.reason: The store artifacts are real and checked in, and the bridge opts in, but no artifact this repository produces loads that bridge: ui/shared/vite.config.ts picks the shell at build time and defaults to generic, and serve-ui serves one go:embed'ed bundle with no flag to serve another. So a user who installs through the platform's own store is still told this is a Docker Compose deployment, which is the defect this check was written to catch. #180 tracks giving serve-ui a way to select a bundle.

storage-picker.reason: Tier B. The shared folder is chosen once at install time through DSM, not browsed from inside the app.

core-binary-hash-parity.reason: This provider consumes the canonical OCI image by reference and checks in no core binary of its own, so there is no second copy of the bytes here to hash against the release manifest. Parity for a provider of this shape is the image reference it names, which canonical-image-parity decides. A cell here can only go green once a provider declares a binaryArtifacts entry and the file behind it hashes to what the manifest recorded.

architecture-parity.reason: This provider makes no architecture claim of its own: it names one multi-arch canonical image and lets the runtime pick. The claim that the built architecture set matches canonical.json is repository-wide and is release-manifest-integrity's row, not seven copies of itself.

native-auth.reason: Tier B. Section 4A gives TrueNAS the generic local auth; no middleware session adapter in v1.

native-notifications.reason: Tier B. Webhooks instead of TrueNAS alerts.

embedded-window.reason: Tier B. The Apps portal link opens the UI in a normal browser tab.

native-notifications.reason: Tier C. Webhooks. PVE notification targets would mean touching the host management plane.

embedded-window.reason: Tier C. Section 4A defers the PVE Web UI plugin indefinitely, so there is no window to embed in.

app-store-packaging.reason: Tier C, and structurally so: Proxmox VE has no third-party application store to package into. That is why this provider is a deployment profile at all.

storage-picker.reason: Tier C. One host directory is shared into the guest and the paths under it are fixed in the env file.
